name: Epilator
lead: An epilator is an electrical device that removes hair by mechanically grasping several hairs at once and pulling them out. The action is similar to waxing, but epilators do not use an adhesive and, unlike waxing, do not remove skin cells [1]. They are used mostly on the legs, arms, underarms and bikini area, with smaller heads for the face.

Because hairs are pulled out of the follicle rather than cut at the surface, the new hair has to grow from beneath the skin before it reappears, and results are described as lasting several weeks, longer than shaving [1][2]. Hair removal reviews classify plucking and related epilation methods as temporary, with only electrolysis labelled permanent [4]. The pulling is painful for many users, particularly on the first sessions; Wikipedia notes that regular epilation of regrowth tends to be less painful than the first treatment [1].
No clinical trials of consumer mechanical epilators have been identified. Evidence comes from general reviews of hair removal, one small electrolysis-related comparison study and user accounts.

Results about 3-6 weeks, similar to waxing [1]

paras: Wikipedia describes four main design families. Spring-type epilators use a flexed coil spring that traps hairs as it rotates; they were the first consumer type and are still sold as manual facial devices turned by hand [1]. Rotating-disc types use metal discs that pinch hairs in a similar fashion [1]. Modern tweezer-type heads use rows of metal plates that move together and apart once per revolution so that hairs are gripped and pulled [1]. Many current models are cordless, rechargeable and designed for wet or dry use in the shower or with a cream or gel, which proponents say reduces pain and irritation [1].
Attachments commonly sold with epilators include small heads for the face and underarms, shaver heads and exfoliation heads intended to be used before and after epilation [1].

Grokipedia describes spring heads as durable and suited to medium and coarse hair but noisy and prone to missing fine hair, tweezer heads as using roughly 20 to 40 small tweezers that can grip hairs as short as about 0.5 mm, and disc heads as quiet and best on straight, fine to medium hair [2]. Common extras include two speed settings, skin guards, massage or vibration attachments and LED lights [2].

The rotating head repeatedly closes and releases around hairs, pulling them out as the device is moved across the skin. Depending on the strength and brittleness of the hair, some break at or just above the surface rather than coming out whole; these can look like sparse stubble, and the number of broken hairs is said to diminish with regular use [1].

Hair grows in cycles, and the proportion of follicles in the growth phase varies across an area. Wikipedia notes that, as with waxing, because of the phases of the growth cycle there is less regrowth after the first epilation [1].

Grokipedia gives an optimal hair length of about 2 to 5 mm for the device to grip, and says repeated use may lead to finer, sparser regrowth, a user-reported effect rather than a measured one [2]. A full-body session is described as taking 20 to 40 minutes [2].

A review of hair removal practices divides methods into depilation (removing the shaft: shaving, chemical depilatories) and epilation (removing the shaft, follicle and bulb: plucking, threading, waxing, sugaring, lasers, intense pulsed light, electrolysis and photodynamic therapy), and states that all methods are temporary except electrolysis, with each having advantages and disadvantages in efficacy and side effects [4]. Mechanical epilators fall within the plucking family of this classification.

A 1998 comparison of three electrical-energy depilation methods (radio-frequency tweezers, direct-current tweezers and needle electrolysis) in ten volunteers reported hair-count reductions of around 56 to 66 percent after nine weeks, with no significant difference between methods but lower pain scores for the tweezer devices [3]. These electrical tweezers are professional-style devices and are different from consumer rotating-head epilators, so the results are an indirect reference only.
Encyclopedic summaries state that results from epilation last up to about four weeks [2].

Wikipedia compares epilators with waxing: both pull hair from the root and are listed with results of roughly 3 to 6 weeks and moderate to high pain; proponents of epilators point to portability and the lack of recurring salon cost, while waxing also removes skin cells and needs hair of a waxable length [1]. Grokipedia contrasts epilation with shaving (results lasting 1 to 3 days), threading (better for precise facial work), laser (reported reductions of 70 to 90 percent over 6 to 8 sessions, best on dark hair and light skin) and electrolysis, which it calls the only FDA-recognised permanent method [2][4].

Pain is the most commonly reported effect. Wikipedia lists approaches that people use to reduce it, including slower speeds, relaxing the skin in a hot shower or bath, using a numbing cream, or having the area professionally waxed first [1]. Redness, ingrown hairs and folliculitis are also described for epilation [2]. A 2023 review of hair removal in the genital area discusses skin reactions and infection risks across epilation and depilation methods generally [5].
Hair removal reviews note that most studies of efficacy and adverse events are limited and based on darker hair and fairer skin [4].

Grokipedia reports that redness, irritation and ingrown hairs can last 24 to 48 hours, that the device works poorly on very fine vellus hair, and that it is not recommended on skin with eczema or active inflammation [2].

The original Epilady, a spring-type device, was released in Israel in 1986 and made by Mepro at Kibbutz HaGoshrim [1]. Grokipedia credits Yair Dar, Shimon Yahav and Menachem Baruch with developing the prototype in 1985 and reports patents in 32 countries [2]. Wikipedia reports that the Remington disc-type epilator led to extensive patent litigation in Europe, including the UK case Improver Corporation v Remington Consumer Product Limited [1]. Wikipedia also notes that a New York Times article by Sabra Chartrand in October 1988 covered the new industry [1].

Later designs replaced the continuous spring and discs with plate-based tweezer heads, and added cordless and wet-use models [1]. Grokipedia dates a rotating-disc model called the Discrette to 1996 [2].

Grokipedia says the Epilady (first marketed as Soft & Easy) mechanised an older manual coiled-spring tool with a small motor, launched in Europe in 1986 and in the US in 1987 at Bloomingdale's in Manhattan, where it reports 1,500 units sold in the first week [2]. It also reports Philips introducing the tweezer-based Satinelle in 1988 and Braun launching the Silk-epil line in 1989, cordless models in the 1990s and shower-use Wet and Dry models in the early to mid 2000s; the same page is inconsistent on some dates [2].
Grokipedia estimates the global epilator market at about 444 million US dollars in 2024, with typical device prices of roughly 25 to over 100 dollars [2].

Epilators are discussed in grooming forums as an option between shaving and waxing: longer-lasting than razors, cheaper over time than salon waxing and usable without heating wax. A thread on the Straight Dope message board compared bikini waxing and epilator use from the perspective of people who had tried both [6]. The site's own rating records the trade-off as weeks of smooth skin at the cost of some pain.

No studies found on consumer mechanical epilators. Related research includes a 1998 comparison of three electrical depilation devices (two tweezer types and needle electrolysis) in ten volunteers [3], and a 1971 German paper on determining hair-root status with a mechanical epilator [7]. General hair-removal literature reviews are summarised above [4][5].
